content.text: Magnets have fascinated humans for thousands of years—from ancient lodestones used for navigation to the powerful magnets in MRI scanners. But what causes magnetism? How do magnets interact? Understanding magnetic fields helps explain compass needles, electric motors, and the invisible forces that affect everyday technology.
Magnets always have two poles (north and south) that come in pairs. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Only iron, cobalt, nickel, and steel are magnetic materials.
Magnetic poles always come in pairs—you cannot have an isolated north or south pole. If you cut a magnet in half, you get two smaller magnets, each with both poles.
Made from steel, ferrite, or rare-earth elements
Become magnetic when near a permanent magnet
Iron is easily magnetised but loses magnetism quickly
This is similar to electric charges, but magnetic poles always come in pairs.

The Earth behaves like a giant bar magnet:
Magnetic north pole is near geographic south pole
Magnetic south pole is near geographic north pole
That's why a compass needle's north pole points north—it's attracted to Earth's magnetic south!
Compass needle aligns with Earth's field
North-seeking pole points towards magnetic north

When drawing magnetic field lines, always remember three rules: lines go from north to south outside the magnet, they never cross each other, and closer lines indicate a stronger field. In exams, forgetting the direction from N to S is a common error.
Two bar magnets are placed end to end. Describe what happens if: a) North is next to south b) North is next to north
a) The magnets attract and stick together. b) The magnets repel and push apart.
A compass is placed near a bar magnet. The compass needle points away from the magnet's north pole. Explain why.

The compass needle's north pole is repelled by the magnet's north pole (like poles repel). The needle's north pole is attracted to the magnet's south pole, so it points towards it (away from the magnet's north).
Describe how to use a compass to plot a magnetic field line.
Place the compass near one pole of the magnet
Mark the position of both ends of the needle (dots)
Move the compass so its back end is at the front dot
Repeat until you reach the other pole or go off the paper
Connect the dots to show the field line
Can be erased by strong magnets
— Only iron, cobalt, nickel (and their alloys) are magnetic. Copper, aluminium, gold are not attracted.
"North pole of magnet points to magnetic north"
— The north-seeking pole of a compass is attracted to Earth's magnetic south pole, which is near the geographic North Pole.
"Breaking a magnet gives separate N and S poles"
— Each piece becomes a complete magnet with both poles.
— They're a model to visualize the field direction and strength. The field exists everywhere, not just on the lines.
— Strong magnets can damage electronics, erase data, and be dangerous if they snap together.

Students often think magnets attract all metals. In fact, only iron, cobalt, nickel, and their alloys (such as steel) are magnetic. Metals like copper, aluminium, and gold are not attracted to magnets at all.

Magnets have north and south poles (always in pairs)
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract
Magnetic materials: iron, cobalt, nickel, steel
Magnetic field: region where magnetic force acts
Field lines: north to south, closer = stronger, never cross
Earth acts as a bar magnet (magnetic poles near geographic poles, but reversed)
Compasses align with magnetic field lines
Induced magnets: temporary magnetism from nearby magnets
Magnetic: iron, cobalt, nickel (or steel). Non-magnetic: copper, aluminium, plastic (or wood, glass).
— Recall from the list of magnetic materials. (recall)
The north pole points towards geographic north.
— Earth's magnetic south pole is near geographic north, so the magnet's north-seeking pole is attracted towards it. (explanation)
Field lines emerge from the north pole, curve around the magnet, and enter the south pole; lines are closest together at the poles (strongest field).
— Apply field line rules: N to S outside, never cross, closer = stronger. (application)
Like poles are facing each other (both north or both south).
The compass needle is a small magnet. Its north-seeking pole is attracted to Earth's magnetic south pole, which is located near geographic north, so the needle points north.
— Earth's core acts as a bar magnet with reversed polarity labelling. (explanation)
Stroke the iron nail repeatedly in one direction with one pole of the permanent magnet. The magnetic domains in the nail align, making it a temporary magnet.
— Induced magnetism through alignment of domains. (description)
The field is strongest at the poles. On a field line diagram the lines are closest together at the poles, indicating higher flux density.
